name: Bonemass maximising

lead: Bonemass maximising is a looksmaxxing term for deliberately building bone mass, the amount and density of mineralised bone, in the hope of a more robust facial skeleton and body frame. Forum guides present bone as living tissue that responds to nutrition, mechanical load, hormones and sleep, and treat childhood and the teens as the key window for reaching peak bone mass.

The appearance chain proposed is: more bone laid down during growth, then thicker cheekbones, jaw and wrists and a more developed frame. Research on bone mass supports the general science of how diet, calcium and loading affect bone and when peak bone mass is reached, but studies measuring visible facial change in healthy people from these habits have not been published.

paras: Guides typically combine a calcium- and protein-adequate diet, vitamin D and vitamin K discussions, resistance and impact training, sleep, and avoidance of smoking and heavy alcohol. Younger members are told the earlier the better, because bone mass accrues most during puberty. Some threads add supplement lists called stacks, and some separate threads discuss prescription drugs or peptides; those are described only as a topic of discussion here.

Diet and exercise elements carry the usual considerations of those habits, such as excess supplemental calcium or vitamin D, which clinicians advise taking only as recommended. The prescription drugs and research peptides mentioned in some guides carry their own side effects and legal restrictions, and several are used in osteoporosis care under medical supervision. Ageing and growth plates set limits on what changes in adulthood.

angle.text: Proponents use bone mass as the foundation for a stronger-looking jaw, cheekbones and frame. The routes people describe are diet, resistance and impact training and sleep, with the biggest emphasis on the teenage years.

lead: Bonemass maximising, often written as bone mass or bonemass, is a practice and discussion topic in looksmaxxing communities about increasing the quantity and density of bone through lifestyle. A widely shared looksmax.org guide describes bone as a living tissue that responds to nutrition, physical activity, hormones, sleep and lifestyle, and argues that genetics play a large part but do not firmly limit potential.[1]

The way it is meant to improve looks is through a chain: adequate nutrition, loading exercise and sleep, especially during growth, lead to more bone mineral and bone size, which proponents link to sturdier cheekbones, jaw, brow, wrists and shoulders and a more developed frame overall.[1] Guides stress that childhood and puberty are the key period for reaching peak bone mass, and describe adulthood as a time of modelling in response to mechanical stress and maintenance.[1]

In the medical literature, peak bone mass is the maximum amount of bone reached in life, typically in the early twenties for women and the late twenties for men.[2] Reviews describe how bone is continually modelled and remodelled in response to its environment, and controlled trials in children have studied calcium supplementation and weight-bearing exercise as influences on bone mineral gain.[3][4][5][6][7][8] The term is part of a wider body of looksmaxxing vocabulary that grew out of online forums in the 2010s and spread to TikTok and livestreaming in the early 2020s.[9]
infobox: Puberty and teens as the main window [1]
Wolff's law: bone adapts to the loads placed on it [5]
Bone density, bone remodelling, osteoporosis prevention

paras: Bone mass in the medical sense is the amount of mineralised bone tissue, usually assessed by size and bone mineral density, and measured clinically by techniques such as dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry.[2][10] In looksmaxxing usage the phrase also stands for visible skeletal robustness. Guides distinguish bone growth in length, which they say ends when the growth plates close, from thickening and density, which they say continue to respond to stress in adulthood.[1]

Threads range from long beginner guides, to requests for help with a stack, to threads aimed at teenagers, to discussions of drugs-only approaches and arguments between members over which methods matter.[11][12][13][14] The most-cited guide opens by saying bone matters for health, strength and appearance, supports muscles, posture and movement, and affects facial structure and body proportions, and that readers should understand the processes involved before trying to raise bone mass naturally rather than relying on drugs and peptides.[1]

The term sits beside other bone-focused topics in looksmaxxing culture, such as mewing and, at the extreme, the widely discussed but rarely practised joke of bonesmashing. Press coverage describes bonesmashing as an inside joke that surgeons warn could cause fractures and nerve injury.[9] Bonemass maximising is distinct from these: its proponents present it as a nutrition and training approach rather than a method of altering the skull directly.

sections.h: Background: how bone responds to load
paras: The scientific idea most often invoked is Wolff's law, formulated by the German anatomist and surgeon Julius Wolff (1836-1902) and set out in his 1892 work on the transformation of bone. It holds that healthy bone adapts to the loads placed on it: increased loading leads a bone to remodel to resist that loading over time, while reduced loading is followed by loss of density.[5] The cellular mechanism is called mechanotransduction, in which osteocytes and other cells sense strain and fluid flow and convert it into biochemical signals; Wolff's law was later refined by Harold Frost's mechanostat model.[5]

Bone remodelling is a lifelong process in which osteoclasts remove mature bone and osteoblasts lay down new bone in basic multicellular units. In adults roughly a tenth of the skeleton is renewed each year, and hormones including parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and growth hormone, together with signalling molecules such as RANKL, regulate the balance.[6] A review of modelling and remodelling in the osteoporosis field describes remodelling as balanced after peak bone mass is reached, with imbalance underlying bone loss.[3]

Looksmaxxing guides draw on this background to argue that bone is not fixed. The step from this general biology to visible change in the facial skeleton is where the practice's specific claims begin, and that step is discussed under research below.

Looksmaxxing as a whole is described in encyclopedic sources as a term that emerged on online forums in the 2010s, including the PSL-rating communities, and that TikTok popularised in the early 2020s, with livestreaming on platforms such as Kick later carrying the more extreme material.[9] Within that culture bone-focused advice has circulated on looksmax.org in the form of long guides, one titled as a 101 introduction, and in repeated threads on stacks, mechanisms and age.[1][11][12][13]

Thread titles show the range of the discussion: a guide on bone mass for beginners, a thread asking whether gains are available at any stage of development, a thread from a 17-year-old asking about options, and a guide devoted to drug-based approaches.[11][15][16][14] Several threads are framed around the growing years, including one from a 17-year-old asking about options.[16]

No single originator is identified in the sources; the practice appears to be a collective forum construct built from standard bone-health advice, sports science on loading and, in some threads, interest in anabolic prescription drugs.

Proponents hold that bone responds to mechanical stress and that heavy lifting, impact and chewing-related loading encourage deposition. They also point to nutrition, noting calcium, vitamin D and protein, and to hormones and sleep as influences.[1] Some members claim that gains are available at any stage of development, while others restrict the idea to puberty.[15]

Several threads emphasise puberty as the stage when the skeleton is most responsive, arguing that habits adopted early have the largest effect on final structure.[1][16] Younger users are advised that the earlier the habits begin, the larger the potential effect, and adults are told that thickening and density can still respond to stress even if length cannot change.[1]

A distinct strand of the community discusses pharmaceutical routes, including bone-active prescription drugs and peptides, and some posts describe them as a faster alternative; the guide authors who favour natural methods explicitly set their approach against these.[1][16][14]

In general terms, guides describe a diet adequate in calcium and protein, discussion of vitamin D and vitamin K, resistance training and impact activities, adequate sleep, and avoiding smoking and heavy alcohol use.[1][4] Some threads present supplement combinations called stacks and ask for feedback on them.[12]

Whether and how these habits affect the visible face varies between accounts. Members mostly post about the habits themselves and about perceived frame changes rather than measurements; no systematic before-and-after data from the community are available.

A 1997 randomised controlled trial and a 1995 controlled trial of bone-active drugs, parathyroid hormone in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and cyclical etidronate in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, examined vertebral bone mass and fracture outcomes in supervised clinical settings.[17][18] These trials concern disease treatment rather than appearance.

In children, a randomised trial in prepubertal girls found that calcium supplementation increased bone mineral gain, and a 2001 follow-up published in The Lancet reported that the difference in bone mass was still present about three and a half years after supplementation stopped, which the authors interpreted as a change in the trajectory of bone mass accrual.[4]

Exercise has been studied extensively as well. A 2007 narrative review of longitudinal and intervention studies concluded that regular weight-bearing exercise appears to enhance bone mineral accrual during growth, that high-intensity jumping appeared beneficial in prepubertal boys and girls, that early puberty may be a particularly responsive window, and that it is unclear how much of the gain persists into adulthood.[8] A 2016 systematic review of nine observational studies in healthy adolescents found eight reporting a positive association between physical activity and bone measures, with the hip showing the most consistent link and the lumbar spine little or none; the authors noted that differing measurement methods prevented a recommended amount of activity.[7]

Public summaries place peak bone mass in early adulthood and note that puberty strongly affects bone size, with males having a longer maturation period than females.[2] Reviews of bone biology describe the cells and signals that couple formation and resorption.[3]

Researchers working on skeletal health focus on bone density and fracture risk, and published studies measuring visible facial bone shape change in healthy people from diet or exercise have not been located. Research on facial ageing describes bone remodelling in the face over decades, but that literature concerns ageing rather than deliberate augmentation.

Diet and exercise elements carry the ordinary considerations of those habits. Health agencies publish recommended intakes and upper limits for calcium and vitamin D and note that exceeding them with supplements can cause problems, so clinicians generally advise following recommended intakes.

Guides that move into drugs and peptides raise the general risks of those substances. Medical literature on drugs that act on bone, such as parathyroid hormone preparations and bisphosphonates, concerns supervised treatment of osteoporosis.[17][18] Some of these are prescription-only and used with monitoring in clinical settings. Posts in which teenagers ask about such drugs have drawn strongly worded replies from other members, showing disagreement inside the community on the topic.[16]
Reviews of exercise and bone in children note that evidence on the best programme and dose is unsettled, and that strong loading in growing bodies is typically studied in supervised settings.[7][8]

On looksmax.org the topic appears as long guides, stack-advice threads and arguments over methods, with heavy emphasis on puberty.[1][11][16] Replies range from praise for high-effort guides to dismissive or joking responses, and the forum's discussions frequently refer to age as the deciding factor for what is achievable.[1][16]

Press coverage of looksmaxxing in general, including The Guardian and BBC pieces in 2024 and major newspaper features in 2026, has focused on more visible practices, with bone-related advice appearing mainly in the context of surgery, mewing and the bonesmashing joke.[9]

No studies found on bonemass maximising as a looksmaxxing practice. Related research on bone mass includes a randomised trial of calcium supplementation in prepubertal girls,[4] reviews of weight-bearing exercise and bone mineral accrual in children and adolescents,[7][8] a trial of parathyroid hormone in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis,[17] and a trial of etidronate in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis,[18] which concern bone density and fractures and not facial appearance.
